summary: Defines the Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info response header fields, used by authentication schemes that need to return information after credentials are accepted. It was replaced by RFC 9110.

eli5.summary: After the guard accepts your ID, he hands you a small note with extra instructions.

questions: how do http authentication schemes return information
subtitle: Response headers for authentication schemes to return server information after credentials are accepted.

tldr.problem: Some HTTP authentication schemes need to communicate additional information to the client after the server has accepted the client's credentials—such as the server proving its own identity or providing session information—but HTTP has no standard header field for this purpose.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7615 defines two response header fields: Authentication-Info for returning authentication-related information, and Proxy-Authentication-Info for the proxy authentication case. Both carry name/value parameters defined by the authentication scheme in use.
tldr.outcome: Authentication schemes can now return post-authentication information in a standard way, generalizing the mechanism previously limited to the Digest authentication scheme. This was later refined by RFC 9110.

today: RFC 7615 is a Standards Track document from September 2015 that obsoletes RFC 2617's definition of these headers. It was later incorporated into RFC 9110, which defines the broader HTTP Semantics. RFC 7615 remains a valid reference and is used by authentication schemes that return post-authentication information to clients.

sections.title: The Need for Post-Authentication Communication
sections.content:
HTTP authentication schemes enable a client to prove its identity to a server. The basic flow is: client sends credentials, server validates them, and responds with the requested resource. But some schemes need to send information after accepting credentials—such as the server proving its identity to the client (mutual authentication), a session token, or parameters the client needs for the next request.

RFC 2617, which defined the HTTP Digest authentication scheme, included two header fields for this purpose: Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info. This RFC generalizes those headers, extracting them from Digest-specific documentation so other authentication schemes can use them too.
sections.eli5: When you show your password, sometimes the server needs to send you back more than just the webpage. It might prove to you that it's really the real server, or give you a ticket you'll need next time. This RFC says how the server should send that extra information.

sections.title: The Authentication-Info Header Field
sections.content:
The Authentication-Info response header field is a list of parameters (name/value pairs), using the same format as authentication parameters in RFC 7235. Each parameter's name and meaning are defined by the specific authentication scheme in use. For example, the Digest scheme defines parameters such as nextnonce, qop, and rspauth in RFC 7616.

The header can be sent in any HTTP response, regardless of the request method or status code. Its semantics are entirely determined by the authentication scheme indicated in the client's original Authorization request header. A proxy forwarding the response must not modify the header field value.

Parameters can be expressed as either tokens or quoted strings, and authentication scheme definitions must allow both formats for interoperability.
sections.eli5: The Authentication-Info header is a list of facts the server tells you after you log in. What facts it includes depends on the type of password scheme. The format is simple: pairs of name and value, either as plain words or quoted text.

sections.title: Proxy-Authentication-Info for Proxy Authentication
sections.content:
The Proxy-Authentication-Info response header field has the same syntax and semantics as Authentication-Info, but applies specifically to proxy authentication (as opposed to origin-server authentication). It is sent by a proxy in response to a client authentication request and conveys information defined by the proxy's authentication scheme.

An important distinction: while Authentication-Info may be forwarded through the proxy hierarchy, Proxy-Authentication-Info applies only to the next outbound client on the response chain—only the client that directly chose that proxy is likely to have the credentials and need the information. However, in some scenarios with multiple proxies within a single administrative domain (such as office and regional caching proxies), each proxy may send the same field value, making it appear as if the header is being forwarded.
sections.eli5: When you connect through a proxy server instead of directly to the website, the proxy might also ask for a password. If it does, it can send back Proxy-Authentication-Info to tell you extra things, just like the website does. But that information is only meant for you, not for proxies downstream.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
Adding information to HTTP responses sent over an unencrypted channel—such as HTTP without TLS—can affect security and privacy. The presence of either Authentication-Info or Proxy-Authentication-Info header fields alone indicates that HTTP authentication is in use, which may reveal information to passive observers.

The contents of authentication-scheme-specific parameters in these headers can expose sensitive information. Authentication scheme designers must carefully consider what information is safe to expose in these headers and may choose to restrict their use to encrypted channels. The RFC does not define specific parameters for these headers; each authentication scheme must document the parameters it uses and their privacy implications.
sections.eli5: If you're not using a secure connection (HTTPS), the extra information the server sends back might be seen by someone listening to your connection. So scheme designers need to be careful about what they put in these headers. Sensitive information might need a locked connection.

sections.title: Standardization and Current Use
sections.content:
RFC 7615 is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 2617. It generalizes the Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info headers from the Digest authentication scheme to be usable by any HTTP authentication scheme. This allows future schemes to return post-authentication information in a consistent, standardized way.

The headers are registered in the IANA Message Headers registry. RFC 7615 was later updated by RFC 9110, which incorporates these definitions into the broader HTTP Semantics specification. Implementations should follow RFC 9110 for the current authoritative definition, though RFC 7615 remains a valid reference for the core concepts.
sections.eli5: This RFC officially says that all password schemes can use these headers, not just the Digest scheme. It was later updated into a bigger RFC about HTTP, but the core idea is the same. Servers can now use this standard way to send back information after you log in.
